2.	If so, when were they issued ?

(Sunday).

Dinner-Soup, roast and boiled meat, boiled ham, roast or boiled poultry, potatoes and vegetables, plum pudding and jelly.
Supper-Cold meats, fried potatoes, preserves. (Monday)
Breakfast-Porridge, mutton chops, cold ham.
Dinner-Soup, Irish stew, roast beef, potatoes and vegetables, pastry.
Supper-Curry and rice, cold meats, chipped potatoes.	[DOT]
(Tuesday).
Breakfast-Porridge, beefsteak, bacon.	'

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine) :

speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the House to go into committee on a certain proposed resolution respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, and the motion of Mr. Puttee in amendment thereto.

Mr. Speaker, there has been so much said on

this question by different hon. members on both sides of this House that it is difficult for one to present any new facts or matters that will be of interest to the House. At the same time I do not feel that I can allow some statements that have been made to pass unchallenged, and I do not care, upon a project of such vast importance to Canada as this is, to give a silent vote. I believe that every man who has taken part in this discussion, that every man who has thereby aided in pressing this scheme forward, that every man,' who records his vote in its favour, will in the future have cause for congratulating himself that the privilege was afforded him here and that he improved the opportunity. In the first place up to a few weeks ago every person almost through the length and breadth of Canada, not admittel, but contended, that this project was absolutely necessary, and that it was an incumbent duty upon the government to proceed at once with the work. I would like to know what would be said of the government to-day by the opposition press if parliament had prorogued without the government bringing down a scheme for another transcontinental road. The whole country, the whole opposition press woull have been up in arms soundly denouncing it, and I believe properly so, because the government would have been recreant to its [DOT]duty if it had not brought down this measure. The project then was necessary, the people demanded it, the country required it, and the only objection that is now taken is that the government has not delayed long enough, that it has not taken sufficient time to obtain the necessary information. Well, I mean to say, Sir, the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House would be very loth indeed to support this scheme were they not convinced that all the information necessary was at hand, t for one would be loth to do so. Do hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House suppose that we have been sitting quietly by all these weeks and months and years, and that we have not possessed ourselves of sufficient information? I mean to state here that my judgment has been convinced that this road Is necessary, and that the government has all the information in its possession for the purpose of entering into the contract that has been made. Now, the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) asked if ever a company had made a contract to build a railroad with such slight information, or if ever a contract for the construction of a railroad had been entered into before instrumental surveys by engineers had been made. I need not go very far afield in answering that question. Let me refer him to a railway at his own doors-the Halifax and South-western Railway. In 1891 the Premier of Nova Scotia entered into a contract with the South-western Railway Company to build a railway from Halifax to
Barrington, connecting with the road to Yarmouth, There had been no survey. There was no such information as we have in regard to this. For years and years the people had been clamouring for the road, and for years and years it had been persistently stated that the road could not be constructed along the south shore of Nova Scotia. When the contract was entered into by the Murray government, what did we find the opposition press and the party, of which my hon. friend is the leader, doing? We found them unanimously denouncing the scheme, we found them stating exactly what the hon. gentleman is stating here, mat the government had not sufficient information, we found them stating that the road could not be built, and we found them stating that the engineering difficulties were insuperable. They denounced the scheme as being wild, reckless and fantastic, and all these phrases that we have listened to coming from hon. members on the other side of the House might have been culled from the opposition press of Nova Scotia at that time. The scheme was presented to the people, these statements were made in regard to it, and what did we find as the answer which the people made ? In the province of Nova Scotia there were returned only two gentlemen as the opposition in the legislature, and I understand that in that province the leader of the opposition, who 'has one man behind him to second his resolutions, is to organize that province in a campaign against that project; and I believe further, if I am informed correctly, that he purposes coming in opposition to the hon. member who spoke to the House last night. That was the position that the opposition took in regard to that railway. What are the facts ? The facts are that the construction is proceeding along the whole line of the road to-day, the facts are that a splendid line has been secured, the facts are that within another year probably the road will be in operation from one end to the other, and that in face of the united opposition of the Conservative party in Nova Scotia, and this road will he built and carried through in spite of their opposition. It is a surprising thing to me when I look back over the history of railroad building in Nova Scotia that we find from the earliest times-and the earliest times were in 1854, when Joe Howe introduced his first railway legislation into the provincial legislature-the Conservative party unitedly denouncing him and denouncing his scheme, and saying that it would bring ruin and destruction to the province of Nova Scotia. Almost continuously from that time forward we have had to meet the opposition of these gentlemen. Let me say in passing, that after this road is built and is successful, I would not be surprised to find these gentlemen on the Conservative benches coming forward and claiming credit for the whole business ; just as they did

after the Dominion coal legislation, which was introduced by my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) in the province of Nova Scotia, the result of which was virtually to save that province from serious financial disaster, and after the Conservative party had denounced it in the press and denounced it on every platform throughout the length and breadth of the province of Nova Scotia.
And in this House.

Yes, and in this House, and after it became an accomplished fact and a huge success and that province was rescued from its financial difficulties; we had then the hon. Sir Charles Tupper running in Cape Breton county and claiming credit for it all-'me, and Betty, killed the bear,' as the old saying goes.
I think it will be incumbent on me to make a few remarks here with regard to the statement made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) last night. Whom the gods wish to destroy they first made mad; and when a man has no argument and feels the weakness of his position, his temper is very near the surface and he is liable to make statements which in his calmer moments he would regret. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) last night saw fit to premise his argument by the statement that the loyalty of the gentlemen upon this side of the House was not all wool or a yard wide, to use his own elegant expression. He made statements reflecting upon the loyalty of the people of his own province of Nova Scotia. He did not stop there, but he made use of these words ;
They were rebels to all intents and purposes.
I wish to tell the hon gentleman now, that those were unwise words. He has stigmatized the majority of the people of Nova Scotia as no better than rebels. He has spoken of the people of Pictou county, the Liberals of Pictou county, as no better than rebels, and yet, Sir, I am informed that every Liberal in the county of Pictou" has at one time or other voted for the hon..gentleman (Mr. Bell). Who was it that first brought forward charges like this in this House and in this country V The hon. Sir Charles Tupper was the first I believe to start the cry. A more unfounded; a more cowardly statement was never made in any place. While he was High Commissioner in England, lie induced the people there to believe that the great Liberal party of the Dominion of Canada were absolutely disloyal to the Crown, and at the time this government assumed power in 1896; at the time when the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made his celebrated speech in Montreal, the English papers next morning announced surprise to find that he was loyal to the empire. Why did they express that surprise V It was because our paid agent in London had been over there slandering us.

Now Sir, I ask, who is the meanest kind of a traitor ; who is the most contemptible kind of a traitor, if it be not the man who charges his fellowmen; who charges the majority of the electors of the Dominion of Canada with being traitors and disloyal. The statements made by Sir Charles Tupper have followed him into oblivion. The position he took in that connection, I believe, has done more to destroy him politically than anything else. And, I wish to say to the hon. gentleman who represents Pictou (Mr. Bell) that I believe that in uttering the words to which I have referred, he was sounding his own political death knell. 1 will say no more upon that subject. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) smiles, but he does not feel happy.
I wish now to address myself to a few of the remarks which were made by my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) with regard to this scheme, it was mighty difficult to find out just where he stood in the matter. He was certain as to all expenditures west-all these gentlemen yonder are satisfied about that; there is no difficulty in their minds about spending millions and tens of millions of dollars all along through the west, through British Columbia, through the wilds of Lake Superior, and even down to North Bay. But then their consciences begin to prick them. They will, some of them, permit expenditure ns far as Montreal, and a few of them will go to Quebec, but not a living soul of them will permit one dollar to be expended beyond Quebec. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) spoke very strongly in favour of the project of the leader of the opposition, until it came down to Quebec. Then he commenced to hedge, but he gave us from his brief facts and arguments which if correct would make it appear that it is absolutely Impossible to construct a road from Quebec to Moncton. That is his argument; that was his array of facts.
He did not say so.
Well, if he did not say so, then my ears misunderstood him entirely.
He said the very opposite.

He pointed out the difficulties of grades, and said that no such road could be built to Moncton because of these grades and these curves, and because of other reasons that I will refer to later. He then quoted or rather misquoted from the report of Sir Sandford Fleming, a report which does not touch this road at all, which was a report upon the building of a road from River du Loup to Truro; and we are not going to River du Loup, and we have been saying that you cannot go to River du Loup. But, Sir, when the hon. gentleman was asked a plain question; when it was put to him fairly and squarely; do you approve of building from Quebec to Moncton; did he answer ? Did this valiant loyal

gentleman make Ms answer to that question in the interest of the maritime provinces 7
Yes he did.
What was his answer.
His answer was
I will tell him his answer; he need not interrupt me.
I must be allowed to state my answer. I answered that I supported the proposition of the leader of the opposition, and that is a straight enough answer.

The answer that the hon. gentleman gave was this :	I will support
the proposition of my hon. friend and leader.
Exactly.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) need not have become restless about this thing. I was not going to quote him incorrectly. X am not intentionally stirring him up.
I want to keep you right.
He said : I adopt the policy of my leader.
Exactly.

Now, what is the policy of his hon. leader with regard to Moncton V As far as I can gather it was that some time in the dim and distant future, when the walking is good around River du Loup, he will go there and see whether there can be a good line obtained, but he has first convinced himself that a good line cannot be obtained, and the whole burden of his argument was to aid and strengthen the contention that a good line cannot be obtained. Therefore, the leader of the opposition does not propose to carry out any such proposition as that, but, as a representative of the lower provinces he dare not take a position flatly and honestly against the construction of the road from Quebec to Moncton. Now, there was a statement made by the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) that this road should have been built long ago from Quebec to Moncton. We have a similar statement from Sir Charles Tupper away back in 1884. We have statements from scores of public men to the same effect, and there is no doubt that the Minister of the Interior was perfectly correct when he said, if the government had to deal with western members instead of members from the maritime provinces, that road would have been built long ago.
I believe that is correct. The hon. leader of the opposition took him to task on this point, and undertook to show that he had cast some reflection on the members from the maritime provinces. Nothing was farther from his mind. What he meant, and what we understood him to mean, and what the country will understand him to 308
mean, is this :	That if there is a matter
of importance or of interest to the west, say to the province of Manitoba-something that is going to build up that part of the Dominion-we would find all the Manitoba members standing together as a unit, and claiming and demanding it. But, Sir, when we are endeavouring to obtain this matter of vital importance to the maritime provinces, do we find all the members from the maritime provinces standing together ? No, Sir ; we have the sad spectacle of the hon. leader of the opposition, who represents the city of Halifax, and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), doing their utmost to discredit that portion of the scheme, and to prevent this road being built to the maritime provinces, though it will be the salvation of the situation so far as those provinces are concerned. That is what the hon. Minister of the Interior meant, and these are the cold, clean facts as demonstrated before this House during the progress of this debate. I wonder why it is that there is such a deadly antipathy on the part of some members on the other side of the House towards the maritime provinces.
Hear, hear.

' Hear, hear,' says that delightful member from Bothwell. He knows what the reason is-will he be kind enough to tell us some day ? That that feeling does exist we know. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that the maritime provinces have a population of about a million. That they are among the older provinces of the Dominion of Canada ; that they have interests to be conserved and looked after ; and I want him and those of his ilk who have this feeling against the maritime provinces, to understand that we of the maritime provinces are determined to protect our rights and to look out for our interests, and that when there is any great scheme before the public for the up-building of Canada, we wish to be in that scheme. We want to be benefited and developed and increased to the same extent as the other parts of the Dominion, if wre can.
Now, I did not take any sectional view of this scheme when it came before the Railway Committee and was discussed there. The position the maritime members took was this, that if a railway was to be built from the Pacific ocean to Quebec, that road railway should be extended through the lower provinces to a maritime province port. We did not ask that any burden should be placed on the western farmer ; we did not ask that he should be compelled to pay one dollar more freight on his grain. But we did say this :	If wei do not Interfere with
the routing of your grain, if we do not add an additional fraction of a cent on the wheat you sent to market, but if at the same time we can cause the shipping of that grain or a portion of it through maritime province ports, we do not think



9S28
you should object. That was the proposition.
Let me refer for a few moments to the history of this movement-and I will be as brief as I possibly can. For years there has been talk of another transcontinental railway. Last year that was crystallized to a certain extent. The hon. leader of the opposition, speaking from his place in parliament, declared that he would support any reasonable scheme for the purpose of providing an outlet for the grain grown in the Canadian North-west. These were his words :
When the hon. gentleman brings down any reasonable scheme for increasing the means of Canadian transportation, any scheme by means of which the grain grown in the Canadian North-west, will be assuredly carried oyer Canadian lines to Canadian ports, and shipped thence to Europe, he will have my support, and I believe the support of every other man on this side of the House.
That was the declaration made by the hon. leader of the opposition upon the floor of this House last session. Now, the scheme has been brought down, but he seems to think that scheme is not worthy of liis support. The first authoritative utterance which we had upon tile project was from the lion. ex-M'inister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), who was the first man apparently on the government side who originated the scheme of another transcontinental railway ; and where did he first launch liis determination on that subject ? Speaking in Vancouver last October, be said that we not only wanted another transcontinental road, but we wanted it right away-almost that evening, he was so much in earnest. Further than that, he said that he was doing his all in order to secure that road, and he led the people to believe, and properly so. that the scheme would be before this parliament at its coming session. All over the Dominion the question of a second transcontinental railway was spoken of. and the newspapers were full of it.
The next tiling that I pause to note is the introduction of the charter of the Grand Trunk racifie Railway Company, and its reference to the Railway Committee. That Bill was presented to the Railway Committee in April, and the first day for the discussion was set for May 7. On that day Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays made their statements before the committee. Upon the 13th day of May there was a strong discussion, in which the maritime members took the position that the railway should be extended from Quebec to Moncton. Reference lias been made to the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific people did not want to build further east than North Bay. and that the extension of the road to Moncton was forced upon them by the government. If that is the case, I sa.v all credit to the government. If they did not allow

the Grand Trunk Pacific to go into the wheat fields of the North-west, and bring the grain down to North Bay and' thence divert the bulk of it to American ports, then I say all hail to the government that prevented them doing that. The position the maritime members took on the 13th of May was this, that if Quebec were made the terminus of the road, that port would be closed for five months in the year. It would be a splendid port for seven months ; but for five months there would be no port at all ; therefore we asked that the road should be extended to a winter port In the maritime provinces. Was this a reasonable proposition or not ? "Would any sensible railway man build a railway across the continent from the Pacific and stop at Quebec ? I say he would not. This is a transcontinental railway, for the purpose of connecting the Atlantic and the Pacific. All these things must be taken into consideration. At the next meeting of the committee the company themselves proposed an amendment to the Bill making Moncton the eastern terminus of the railway. The hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals stated here the other day that that amendment was proposed by somebody who wanted to kill the scheme. Surely the hon. gentleman should not have made that statement, because he was sitting next beside the chairman of the Railway Committee at the very time the company moved the resolution themselves to extend the line down to Moncton.
1 want to draw attention to the position taken by my friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) before the Railway Committee. I find him reported in the St. John ' Sun ' to have said, and the report corresponds with my recollection with what took place :
Mr. Bell insisted on the Bill being placed in such a form so as to meet the wishes of the maritime provinces, who were almost unanimous in the opinion that the road must have its terminal at a Canadian port.
My hon. friend I suppose will not doubt the accuracy of this report. That was his position before the Railway Committee. What was the position of some others ? Let me refer to the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hale) while that project was before the Railway Committee, they sent this telegram to the St. John Board of Trade :
Important that civic bodies take immediate united and strong action re Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Apparent intention is to make Portland winter terminus, and if maritime provinces are to reap the reward for past sacrifices, a fight to the finish must be made.
That was the position taken by these two hon. gentlemen, and I believe that it was in consequence of that position the Board of Trade of St. John send the following telegram. or rather the mayor of St. John :

St. John, N.B., May 13. Charles S. Hyman, M.P.,
Chairman Railway Committee,
Ottawa.
The following resolutions were unanimously adopted by the common council of the city of St. John this morning :
Resolved, that the city of St. John has heard with regret that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company indicate an intention to build its line from the Pacific to the city of Quebec only and do not propose to construct and extend the same so as to have during the winter season a terminus at the open sea on Canadian soil. Which means that the company will do all its transatlantic business in winter through United States ports. And further resolved that such a course of procedure would do great injustice to the 'maritime provinces' and would be applying the money and resources of Canada to the upbuilding of a foreign city and port.
And still further resolved that this city respectfully, earnestly and most strenuously urges' the representatives in parliament from the city and county of St. John and from the province of New Brunswick and the maritime provinces generally to do all in their power to protect the interests of their provinces in the matter of preventing the injury that would be done if the proposed wrong should be carried out. And further resolved that the necessary protection against this impending injustice should be placed in the Act incorporating the company, should any such be passed.
And still further resolved that this city requests the representatives of Quebec, Ontario, and the other more western provinces and territories to so act in securing such protection that the road to be built by the company shall pass from ocean to ocean through Canadian territory in both -winter and summer and that such measures may be taken as will ensure the carrying through Canadian ports only of all freight originating or desired for any part of the Dominion of Canada.

Mayor.
That is wliat the city of St. John thought of the matter. On the 20th of May, my lion, friend the leader of the opposition, who had for some time been periodically questioning the government as to when they were going to bring down their scheme, again interrogated them. Everybody knew that there was a government scheme to come as a corollary to the charter which went through the House, and frequently my hon. friend claimed the right to know "when this scheme was coming forward. On the 26th of May he had become so imp-patient that he impressed this House with the idea that the moment a scheme would be launched for the construction of a transcontinental railway, so earnest was he in his desire to have that work carried forward that he would leave his place in parliament, seize a pick and shovel, and hasten to work on the construction of the road itself. Let us see what he said on the 26th of May. He put his question to the First Minister, and premised it by quite a long speech. In that speech he told us that the whole country was clamouring for this railway. that the boards of trade, city councils
308i
and so forth all over the Dominion, from one end to the other, had passed resolutions demanding the building of this road, and he proceeded to read a resolution which had been passed by the board of trade of the city of Halifax. That resolution was as strong as any resolution could be in favour of building this road and in favour of Moncton. He also stated that the then Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) had received a strong telegram from the St. John Board of Trade to the same effect. I shall just cite a few words from the speech of the lion, gentleman :
Now. there is a strong feeling in the country, and particularly in the maritime provinces, and one that the government should especially keep in mind, that the government should insist on guarantees that the termini of any road to which government assistance is given shall be within the limits of the Dominion of Canada. Public meetings have been held, boards of trade have passed resolutions, municipal bodies have passed resolutions, not only in the maritime provinces, but throughout the length and breadth of Canada, insisting on this condition. Indeed. I am led to mention this matter to the House now because of a resolution which has iust been placed in my bands passed by the Halifax Board of Trade, and which I will take the liberty of reading to the House.
I shall not read the whole of the resolution, but here is a part of it:
And further resolved, that this board protests against government assistance of any kind being granted to any transcontinental railway unless a distinct and binding condition is enforced that said railway shall be built entirely on Canadian territory, and its export and import traffic shall be through Canadian termini, and that the rates of freight charged by said railway shall be as low via the ports of St. John, K.B., and Halifax, N.S., as rates charged via any port on the Atlantic seaboard.
And further resolved, that if aid is asked from the Canadian government by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway the interests of the maritime provinces should be safeguarded by compelling this railway company to commence the construction of the eastern portion of its line at Moncton, N.B., and complete it as far as the city of Quebec.
That is the resolution of the board of trade of the city of Halifax, in the c:unty represented by the leader of the opposition, and in presenting that resolution, lie prefaced it by remarks which showed that it had his entire sympathy, and I believe that at that time he was in sympathy with the purpose of that resolution and with the building of a road to Moncton.
A.i hon. MEMBER. He is now.

Perhaps he is, I cannot tell, but the exigencies of party have made him give other utterances. Upon this occasion he also read a telegram, which he said the then Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) had received from St. John. I do not know how it comes that on the 26th of May, the hon. the leader of the opposi-

tion was in a position to know the contents of a telegram to the then Minister of Railways and Canals. But he says that the exminister did receive this telegram, and I am prepared to take his word for it. Here it is :
Unless the Grand Trunk Pacific build their line through to some maritime province port we believe the export business will continue to go through an American port as in the past.
Mr. Hays rightly says shippers can route freight as they please and if the Grand Trunk are interested in route via Portland, shippers can be easily influenced to route practically every ton of export freight that way.
We cannot believe that any arrangement can be made

Here is the important part of it :
-between Intercolonial and Grand Trunk which will prevent this.
We urge in the strongest terms that no government assistance be granted to any transcontinental railway that does not undertake to build their line through to some maritime province port.
And, Sir, in the face of all these things, in the face of the declarations of the leader of the opposition, in the face of the speech made by the ex-Minister of Railways in Vancouver, in the face of all these representations from municipal councils and boards of trade, we had the ex-Minister of Railways standing in his place in parliament, declaring there was no one who wanted this road to Moncton except the people who hoped to make money out of its construction. It was a very strong remark to make against the province of New Brunswick, and I do not wonder that the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) resented it, as he did properly resent it in making his speech. I have only a few words more to say with regard to this Moncton business, and then I have finished. The ex-Minister of Railways contends that he left the cabinet because he believed that the construction of this part of the road would destroy the Intercolonial, and we have heard hon. gentlemen on the other side, taking their cue from him, declaring in the most pitiful tones that we are going to slaughter the people's railway. Have you heard one solitary member on this side of the House say anything against the Intercolonial or say that the Intercolonial would be injured by this road ? Not one. And I mean to say here that not only will the Intercolonial not be injured by the construction of this road to Moncton, but it will be benefited. And I will take occasion, before I resume my seat, to prove that to the satisfaction of every hon. gentleman present. But because the ex-minister is so convinced, he says, on that score, he resigned his seat in the cabinet. It is fair for me to see what he has said on other occasions. A few years ago, a charter was given to construct a railroad from St. Charles Junction at E6vis, to Connor station, near Ed-

mundston, and a subsidy was granted to this road. Subsequently, in the year 1901, there was a change desired in the western terminus of the road, and a resolution was introduced to allow the road to go either to St. Charles Junction or to Chaudiere. A discussion arose over this Bill. Be it remembered that this road runs substantially over the route of the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific from Chaudi&re to Connor, near Bd-mundston. There is no doubt about that. It has been surveyed ; the plans and profiles are in existence, and we know all about the country. Now it is well to see what position the ex-Minister of Railways and some other hon. gentlemen on the other side took with regard to that road. The first I will refer to is the hon. and valiant member from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes). Some hon. gentlemen had taken the position that this road would parallel the Intercolonial and interfere with the traffic. What does the hon. member for Victoria say ?
This will be another through Canadian Pacific Railway line, and when the new bridge is completed at Quebec the Canadian Pacific Railway will then be able to use its line on the north shore in connection with this line as an additional through-road to the sea.
But, though this was the hon. gentleman's position in 1901, to-day we have him telling us that it is impossible to build a road through that country, and, if it were built, the grades would be so tremendous that it would be impossible for it to carry any through-traffic. He spent hours and hours perusing the geological survey reports, and he has discovered that there are mountains in that country. He shows us that there are scores of hills there. Well, I suppose he has seen some hills and mountains elsewhere, and he has seen railways running along the base of those hills. This just shows the inconsistency of these hon. gentlemen. Bast year or the year before, they were all in favour of building this road, but to-day, when it is part of the government policy, they change their minds. The next man I will refer to is the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler), who said :
While it is important that nothing should he done to interfere with the Intercolonial Railway, it is more important we should find the shortest means of communicating to the wrest and the seaboard.

Solicitous and all as he is, and solicitous as I would naturally be, in relation to anything that would he harmful to the Intercolonial Railway, I would not hesitate to give support and assistance to this project, and in doing so would not feel that I was infringing in the slightest de-

gree on the interests of the Intercolonial Railway. These people have no railway communication. They have a very fine country, as I understand it, and they ought to have railway communication. He came here on the 18th of August, and he told us that he had been studying this question about four or five weeks, and then he proposed the scheme that he has proposed.
In the meantime, while he was away preparing this scheme, this great measure, this great act of constructive statesmanship as it has been termed, his followers were left here alone, and they supposed that they would be doing the correct thing in following the lead of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), and they did so, and for this they should not be blamed by the leader of the opposition. They followed the hon. ex-Minister of Railways loyally, echoing his every sentiment. The scheme proposed by the government has been so fully discussed that I shall refer to it only in the briefest possible manner. The first stipulation in connection with it is that the company shall deposit with the the government $5,000,000 in cash. Now, do hon. gentlemen suppose for one moment that business men would deposit $5,000,000 in the hands of the government, where they might lose every cent of it, simply for amusement ? Do these gentlemen, who have now become experts in railway management, railway operation and steamship operation, and who would have us believe that they know worlds about the freight rates and the tolls and the combinations- would these gentlemen set up their judgment against the judgment of the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway. If we were to listen to them we would conclude that that man is a lunatic and' does not know what he is doing. He talks about hauling the freight from the west over his railway but these gentleman say it cannot be done; the leader of the opposition says that it cannot be done. Well, if that be true, I must ask him to go to the debates of 1881, and read the speech of Sir Charles Tupper and the speeches of others on his side. Sir Charles Tupper then told the country, and he justified his bargain with the Canadian Pacific Railway by stating, that that road could carry all of the wheat produced in that vast

country of some two hundred odd million acres. That was the position which he assumed and that was the position assumed by all the supporters of that measure at the time. The government of that day desired fo make use of the water stretches but Sir Charles Tapper said that could not be done. And a greater man than Sir Charles spoke on that occasion. In 1881 he said :
The question is one of the utmost importance to the country from whatever point of view it be considered. If we consider the fact that the road will be a great commercial thoroughfare through a country that is over 4,000 miles long, that it will carry the trade of an area of country that consists of over 250 millions of acres of land, we cannot fail to regard the subject as of surpassing interest to the people of this country.
Then he justifies his not putting it before the electors. He said it was not necessary to put it before the electors and goes on to say :
The people finally concluded that the water stretches were only a sham. In every instance, when I have been able to take the sense of the people, I have invariably found that it was their desire to have the railway built by a company, and not by the government.
And so on. But I think the richest part of his whole speech is where he says that the building of this road was most important, because it would double the debt of the Dominion.
Now, the hon. member for East Grey upon this occasion followed the lead of all the others in saying that the waterways were a sham and could not be utilized. To-day we have him coming back here and saying that we must revert to the waterways.
Another witness has been brought forward here, I refer to Sir William Van Horne. It seems that the Canadian Pacific Railway are taking some interest in this question. One of the directors of that com-pany\has made a speech in this House, to which lam going to refer in a little while, but Sir William Van Horne, speaking in New York last year in regard to the Trans-Canada line said :
Canada, he said, has been adding sides to her hopper for a long time, but has neglected to enlarge the spout. She has for many years Mr. WADE.
been spending millions generously in the development of the interior, and her railways, but has neglected her outlet at the Atlantic. He approves the Trans-Canada line in these words. He was asked what effect the building of the Trans-Canada line would have on the Canadian Pacific Railway and he replied :

The position of the Canadian Pacific Railway is absolutely unassailable. For that reason it is our policy never to oppose anything. The Trans-Canadian road has started with better prospects than the Canadian Pacific had once. When the Northern Pacific road was built, every body thought it was away up north beyond nowhere. Then the Great Northern was built and people promptly forgot thinking of the Northern Pacific as far north. Then came the Canadian Pacific, and that seemed to run through the Arctic regions. We would hail with delight a parallel route from the Atlantic to the Pacific to help us develop the country. [DOT] There is enough of it up here for us all.
That was tbe position taken by Sir William Van Home in this interview in New York. Let us see what he had to say the other day. In a recent interview he says :
Neither the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway nor any other allCanadian route,' said Sir William, ' will ever voluntarily carry a carload of wheat by the all-railway route around the great lakes to an eastern Canadian port for shipment abroad, for the simple reason that it will never pay any road to do so. Nor will the transportation problems in the west ever be solved by the construction of an all-Canadian route from coast to coast.'
Continuing, Sir William stated :
The Canadian Pacific Railway shipped every carload of wheat that it was possible to ship by their steamship line on the great lakes from Fort William to Owen Sound, and thence east' by rail, or else by way of Buffalo and the Erie Canal.
In the first place, he stated in this interview that he would hail with delight a second transcontinental railway, and in the second interview he says that such a line is not necessary, and tells us that they cannot haul wheat around the north shore of Lake Superior. If Sir William Van Horne would content himself to speak of his own road, I would not quarrel: he would be quite right. The Canadian Pacific Railway, as constructed around the north shore of Lake Superior, could not and cannot carry grain. Why ? Because the grades are too heavy.
It is not a heavy freight carrying road.
It cannot be built for such a purpose. That is the reason. Let me refer the hon. gentleman for a moment to this question of gradients and show what an important part it

plays. I am referring to * Tire Economic Theory of Railway Location,' by A. M. Wellington. Here we will find a table which shows the relative resistance of gradients. A locomotive which would draw 250 tons on the level would, with a four-tenth gradient, only be able to draw 125 tons, with a 1 per cent gradient it would only he able to draw 7i -43 tons, and with a 1 -20 per cent gradient it would only be able to draw 62-50 tons. That shows how important these gradients are, and I assume that the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, in constructing this road, will have that in view. It is a matter of mutual agreement between them as to the kind of road that is to be built, but the purpose has been determined upon, and that is to provide a road that will bring out the grain from the west. If that is done, it will be a road with what is known as normal gradients of four-tenths of one per cent as the maximum gradient. There may be short places on the road where you may get a stiffer grade than that, and where the momentum of the train would carry you over it, but where there is a long gradient, it should not be greater than four-tenths of one per cent. I believe that under this project of the government a line with the maximum gradient of four-tenths of one per cent can be secured. It may be a surprise to some lion, gentlemen opposite to know that in the course of two or three weeks there will be an instrumental survey completed from Winnipeg to Lake Abitibi, and that the engineers will report having secured a line with that maximum gradient If a road is built of that description from Winnipeg to Moncton, I cannot believe any man would stand here and say that grain cannot be carried to the maritime seaports. I believe that it can be carried there, I believe it will be carried there, and Mr. Hays, the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, believes that it will be carried there. At any rate, representing a constituency in the maritime provinces, I think I am justified in giving him an opportunity to try the experiment of building that road there. I do not believe it is an experiment. ail the same. I think it is a fact, a certainty, that if you build the road from Winnipeg to Moncton of the nature and character that I have described the grain of the west will be brought down to the maritime ports. I believe that the bulk of the grain will be shipped from St. .Tolin, and I believe that Halifax will get her compensations in the manner which I will state hereafter. This is the contract which has bten entered into between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I shall not go over the different provisions of it, because I dare say hon. gentlemen are tired of it, but I will refer to the scheme which has been propounded to the House by the hon. leader of the opposition as an alternative scheme. Many
of the figures in connection with this have been given to the House, but I will find it necessary to go over them, as mine are somewhat different, and proceed upon a somewhat different basis. If, however, the Canada Atlantic Railway commends itself to the judgment of experts, and from what information I can obtain with regard to it, I should think it ought so commend itself, and I would think that the extension of the Intercolonial Railway between Co-teau and Jacques Cartier Junction, and the acquisition of the Canada Atlantic Railway to Depot Harbour, would place the Intercolonial Railway in a very much better position than it is at present.
First of all, I would like to know how that will place the Intercolonial Railway in any better position? The Canada At-antic Railway to-day is doing a certain business. or nineteen days, has evolved a scheme by which he proposes to do it. My hon. friend would also have to deepen and equip the harbours.
