The government will have a first lien on the road on account of the guarantee on the other three-fourths of the cost of construction. The Grand Trunk will then have a second mortgage only to answer for their guarantee on the remaining fourth. Should the Grand Trunk Pacific neglect to operate the eastern section, and should the government, who are surely in earnest, apply the means at their disposal to force the company to fulfil its obligations, the Grand Trunk, having only a second charge on the road, would be the loser. Is it not a fact that the Grand Trunk would suffer loss, in case the Grand Trunk Pacific Company did not operate the eastern section, and as a consequence was sued by the government and turned over to a receiver ? For all these reasons, we are bound to come to the conclusion that the company with whom the government have been dealing are in earnest and anxious to carry out the agreement.
Now, as to the price, I shall say a few words only. The amount of money which this country will have to pay for the building of this transcontinental road is exceedingly small ; and those who are in a position to know, can hardly 'believe that the government of Canada has made such a good bargain. But the contract is'there all the same, and the railway will be built.
There is no doubt that the mortgage secured by the government on the western section of the road will ensure the full recovery of the government's outlay, should the company be unable to pay. It is admitted by all that the western part of the road will be paying. There is a certainty, as a consequence, that the government will have absolutely nothing to pay. Now, as regards the eastern section, the amount of three per cent to be paid at the expiry of seven or ten years will represent the Interest to be paid by the government. So, the government will have to pay seven years' interest on the eastern section, and seven years' interest on the Rocky Mountains' section. As stated by the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior, the whole amount will come to thirteen or fourteen million dollars. To build a transcontinental road at an expenditure of thirteen or fourteen millions, seems to me quite a feat, and I am confident the whole country will endorse such a transaction. But reference is made to

liabilities to be met at the expiry of fifty years, on the bonds quaranteed by the gov, eminent. It is true that the government will have to pay for the debentures issued on the eastern section ; but it should not be forgotten that in fifty years from now the population of Canada will have reached the twenty or twenty-five million mark; that the revenue will be much larger than it is to-day ; that the road will be a paying one, and that instead of receiving three per cent, the government will be getting six or eight per cent, and the difference between the two rates of interest will be used as a sinking fund during the fifty years to follow. I may add that the road will remain the property of the government.
There are other clauses on which * sl all not dilate, but which it will suffice to mention in order to show the advantages ensured by this scheme. Thus, the government have reserved over that part of the road which is leased running rights for themselves and for other railway companies. Nor should we lose sight of the other clause which states that the material required for the construction of the railway shall be purchased in Canada whenever the company are able to secure them on terms as advantageous as in foreign countries. Let me also recall the right which the government have reserved of controlling the rates. That is an invaluable concession, aad of great benefit to the country. In conclusion, let me say this : It is the opinion of fa r-m.idrd people, of those whose views are not biassed by a spirit of partisanship, but who are rather inclined to consider the scheme on its merit, that this arrangement is an admirable one. I for one, do not hesitate to say that the government have succeeded in making a great bargain, such as is seldom concluded, especially by governments. As against the views of papers who are interested in finding fault with the policy of the government whatever it be, we have those of persons whose minds are not influenced by party spirit. The other day, I was reading the following item from the New York 1 Journal,' Reproduced in the ' Canada.'
A railroad is to be built in Canada parallel to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and which is to be called the Grand Trunk Pacific. The new road will in no way interfere with its old competitor, but will only help In developing the country, and bringing about good results for both roads. Within the next ten years the development of the Dominion of Canada will astonish the whole world. The products of the farms, the fisheries, the forests and the mines have increased by 283 per cent, and the manufactured goods by 738 per cent, under the Liberal rule.
Let me, Sir, draw your attention, in passing to the views expressed by the ' Moniteur du Commerce,' published in Montreal. That paper frankly supports the scheme propounded by the government. Such utterances have more weight than criticisms from opponents of the cabinet.
As regards the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), urging that the government should acquire and operate the railways, and should build and run the proposed road, I believe that principle is a wrong one. . It is a good plan for the government to grant help towards building railways or to take charge of such work, but I consider the operation of railways by the government a source of danger. For that reason, I shall vote against that amendment.
The proposed road, to my mind, will be a benefaction to the whole of Canada. I am satisfied, Sir, that the province of Quebec, like the other provinces, will be benefited thereby. In my opinion a transcontinental railway that would have its terminal at North Bay, would not be of much good, and we from the province of Quebec would not have supported such a proposal. The province of Quebec and the maritime provinces contribute liberally to the expenditure made to ensure the development of the North-west. We do not object to that ; but when a transcontinental railway is being built, we want all the provinces to be benefited thereby. We rejoice at the government having decided to build a railway that will run through all the provinces of Canada.
Under the circumstances, I believe, Sir, that every member of this House who is anxious to help on conscientiously the interests of the country, heedless of party, should support this Bill. It Is a bold undertaking, perhaps, but worthy of the progressive government which control the affairs of the country. It was conceived in a lofty spirit of public interest, and let us hope that it will be carried out in the same spirit. And if it is, we may rest assured that the whole country will greatly profit by it, and that It will be one of the most efficient means of development for the next fifty years.

MACLAREN (North Perth.) Mr. Speaker, I have one great regret, and that is that I cannot answer in the French language the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. His speech will not be criticised very much by me because I do not understand a single word he has said.
I am very sorry for you.

I do not think I would have said a word on the proposition which is now before the House had It not been for the fact that last session I spoke at some length upon the transportation question, and I feel it incumbent upon me to make a few remarks now upon the Grand Trunk Pacific project, which has formed the subject of this debate. Before proceeding further, I wish to present to the House resolutions passed by the board of trade of the city of Stratford and other parties. This is a copy of a resolution adopted by the Stratford board of trade at a meeting held on the 3rd of April, 1903 :

Moved by Mr. Wm. Preston, seconded by Mr. W. J. Mooney-
Whereas the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have made application to the Dominion parliament for power to build a transcontinental line of railway from Quebec city to a point at or near North Bay, and thence to the Pacific coast, and
Whereas the said company* have expressed their intention to ask for a cash subsidy to enable them to carry out the proposed work, and
Whereas the new railway will open up a Very large and important section of Canada not at present available for settlement, or served by any railway, thus contributing largely to the growth, development, and general welfare of Canada, and
Whereas it is desirable that these lands should be opened up and settled as soon as possible, therefore
Be it resolved, that in the opinion of this board, while not expressing any views on the general principle or railway subsidies, we believe it to be in the interests of the Dominion of Canada considering the magnitude of the new railway, and to insure its rapid completion, and the early settlement of our unoccupied lands, that a reasonable subsidy be granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
That a copy of this resolution be presented to the Hodse of Commons, through our repre sentative. A, P. MacLaren, M.P.

Secretary.
That is the first resolution which I wish to present to the House. Then, I have another from the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, which is as follows :
Stratford, May 6, 1903.
Dear Sir.-I beg to forward you in behalf of the membership of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Fireman, resident in Canada, east of St. Clair river, the following resolution.
Whereas, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has made application to the Dominion parliament for power to build a transcontinental line of railway from Quebec city to a point at or near North Bay and thence to tho Pacific const
Whereas, the said company expresses their intention to ask for a subsidy to enable them to carry out the proposed work.
Whereas, the new' railway will open up a very large and important section of Canada not at present available for settlement or served by any other railway which if built, will thus contribute largely to the growth, development and general welfare of Canada.
Whereas, it is desirable tha>
these lands should be opened up and settled as soon as possible.
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of the membership of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Fireman, resident in Canada, while not wishing to express any views on the principle of railway subsidies, we believe it to be in the interests of Canada, considering tho magnitude of the new railway and to insure its rapid completion and the early settlement of our unoccupied lands, that a reasonable subsidy be granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
In conclusion, we sincerely invite you to accept this resolution because we earnestly believe the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will open up a section of new country that will Mr. MACLAREN (Perth).
develop so rapidly that many deserving young men and women will find homes and employment in that portion of undeveloped Canada.
I remain.
Yours respectfully,

Secretary.
I have another resolution signed by Mr. M. D. Hunter, from the joint general committee of adjustment of conductors and brakemen of the Grand Trunk system east of the St. Clair river, which is in the same terms as those which I have already presented, and I shall not, therefore, trouble the House by reading it. Now, the House will see by these resolutions1 that they were dated away back in April and May, at a time when the bodies from which these resolutions come had no thought whatever of such a tremendous project being brought before parliament as that which has been presented by the right hon. leader of the government. At that time they thought it was simply a case of connecting the present ends of the Grand Trunk Railway with the two oceans, and they had no thought, as I have said, of such a tremendous undertaking as that which has been proposed. As far as X am personally concerned, I would have supported the granting of any reasonable assistance to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and particularly assistance in extending the road west of Lake Superior into the great wheat fields and ranches in Manitoba and the North-west Territories and to the mines, the fisheries and the forests of British Columbia. I certainly would have been willing to grant any reasonable assistance to the company for this purpose, and as far as I am concerned, I would be inclined to support the building of all the railways that are necessary to open up and develop the country west of Lake Superior. I spoke last year at some length on the developing of the waterways from the head of Lake Superior down to points along the Georgian bay and Lake Huron, such as Collingwood, Owen Sound, Midland, Sarnia, Goderich and Windsor, and I still hold the views which I ex-' pressed then. I have not changed my mind as to that. I think these waterways should be improved, and I think, as many hon. members on this side of the House have said during the last few days, that the ports on our inland waters should be built up, that we should have first-class elevators constructed on modern principles, that we should have properly equipped warehouses and in some parts cold storage where perishable goods could be unloaded, stored and then shipped by rail. As I said last year, I think it would tie well if some assistance were granted to the parties who hold charters for the construction of a road from Collingwood to Toronto. If such assistance were granted it would enable shippers' to utilize the waters from the head of Lake Ontario, because, if there was a sufficient

freight supply from the west we would have steamers running from the head of Lake Ontario to the seaboard. If some of the traffic from the North-west could be secured for'such a route we could have a magnificent fleet of steamers sailing from Toronto to the sea. I think the sooner the government go to work and improve the waterways, while at the same time lowering the rates, the better it will be for the people.
X may say here, Mr. Speaker, that I have not changed the views which I expressed here last year, and I still think that the government should do something for the manufacturer and for the horny-handed sons of toil, who have hewed down the forests of this country and who have spent their lives in building up this country. They are the men to whom this government should first look and for whose benefit they should spend some of their money before opening up too much new country at such a tremendous outlay as that which is proposed in this measure. My idea is that if the government spent one-tenth of the amount of money in improving our waterways, more good would be accomplished than if they expended the $150,000,000 or $200,000,000 involved in this project. I do not think the country is ripe for such an expenditure or that it is prepared to assume liability for so many millions of dollars. I certainly think, as a business man, that the people who have built up the different provinces should receive some consideration. I do not say Ontario particularly, because I take a broad view of these questions. I would like to see every province prosper and I want to see every province derive its share of benefits from the expenditure of public money. I do not want to take a narrow view or to say that one province is jealous of the other. ' I never had any feeling against any province in the Dominion of Canada. On the contrary, I have the most kindly feel

ing towards all the provinces, and I would be sorry to see any hon. member of this House attempting to stir up any feeling between the different provinces. We are all one. As far as the maritime provinces are concerned, I am very glad to know that we have a magnificent market in that part of the country for many of our manufactured goods and agricultural products, and I think the maritime provinces have a kindly feeling towards the province of Ontario. I am glad to know that the province of Ontario reciprocates any such feeling and I think hon. members on both sides of the House will agree with me when I say that such a feeling should exist all along the line.
Now, a great many people talk about making Winnipeg a great centre, and they say that Winnipeg is going to become a great manufacturing centre. It certainly is a great city to-day, but I think that Fort Arthur and Fort William will become very important distributing points in the near
future. At the present time when the steamers arrive there;, they unload their goods through the freight sheds into the cars, the goods are hauled by rail to Winnipeg, unloaded there, carted up town, warehoused; the goods are sold by the wholesale men, then carted to the station again and shipped to different points all over Manitoba and the North-west Territories. I think it would be a wise step on the part of the government to assist in the building of warehouses at Port Arthur and Fort William and making these places the great forwarding points for the west. It would be a great saving in time and labour. It would save extra handling, extra haul and extra labour generally. I think that would be an important question for the people of the west to work out and I do not think it would do the city of Winnipeg much harm.
Now, in regard to the proposed road from Collingwood to Toronto, there are people who express the view that it would not pay, but as Collingwood is 300 feet higher than Toronto the grain could be shipped across very cheaply and if the most modern type of elevator were used it could be handled in the most economical way. There are only about six or seven miles upon which a serious grade would be encountered, but two engines could be employed at this place to haul the trains and a good speed could be maintained.
Since the government has so much money, I would like to see some of it expended in utilizing the water-powers and in building electric roads through that part of the province of Ontario lying west of Toronto, where, I believe, there are already twenty-one charters for electric roads. On these roads cheese, butter, grain, cattle, hogs, anything at all produced or manufactured in that district could be brought to Toronto. They could be stored in Toronto and shipped by boat in the summer time, or if they were not shipped by water, a lower rail rate could be obtained. In this way freight rates could be materially reduced. We all know that the rates are very high in the Ontario peninsula and in the west, and I would like to see warehouses, cold storage plants and elevators of the largest and most improved style, such as are to be found in Duluth. Chicago, Boston and Philadelphia, erected for the storage of produce. If the Americans can do this kind of wo"rk, there is no reason why we should be behind them and why we should not. by these means, get as low a rate of freight as do the people to the south of us. I think that it is much more important that relief should be given to those who are doing all this great and good work for the development of the country now than to spend money to open up an unknown and uninhabited country, which, as one hon. gentleman said the other day, is now known only by the birds.

If these great waterways were utilized, we could not only ship our produce clean down to the sea, but we could bring back as return cargoes, coal and iron and also secure for Canadian lines that great foreign trade which now comes into New York and Boston and is brought west via Niagara, whence it is sometimes sent right through to Winnipeg and to all points in western Ontario. These goods we could haul up through our own country and we could have them distributed from Toronto, Owen Sound, and different points in the North-west, This, I think, is another strong argument in favour of utilizing our own waterways. Why wait one moment to relieve the people who have done all this good work ? Talk about waiting to open up this new country ! A year ago I asked the government to do something to reduce these high rates of freight throughout the western country. At that time we were promised a commission; we have been promised that commission for many years, and I understand it has now been appointed. The first thing that this commisison should do is to look into the possibility of lowering the rates of freight charged the people who are doing business now, not wait for those people who may be doing business in that new land when this railway is built, but to secure lower rates for our present producers, so that they will be able to compete with the rest of the world. The Prime Minister says : We cannot wait, we cannot wait. There is no one in this new land to wait But the great manufacturers of our older and thickly settled portions of this great Dominion can wait. These can wait, and then when this great road is built through an uninhabited land, it will not relieve the people or lower the rates on freight one cent as far as such commodities as butter, cheese, lumber, furniture, coal, &c., are concerned. I believe in giving now. If you have anything to give give it to the people who have done so much for the development of Canada, and do not wait to bring in new people and then help them. Give it, as I have said, to the people who have developed this country.
We have heard a good deal about an allCanadian route and about shipping our goods through Canadian ports. I fully agree with every bit of that, and would "like to ship everything that I buy in Canada and ship to the old country through Canadian ports. I hope the day will come when it will be possible to ship it all in that way. But is is useless to talk about that when the Americans give better rates. For instance, when I buy cheese in the west, the first thing I do is to wire to Montreal, Boston, New York and other ports asking the lowest rate for the goods to London, Liverpool, Bristol, Glasgow, or whatever point I want to ship to, and I, of course, ship all things by the route which gives the cheapest rate of freight, and the lower the Mr. MACLAREN (Perth).
rate I obtain the higher price I can pay to the farmer for what I buy from him. Let us make our Canadian railways and waterways right and then we can get cheaper and lower rates by a Canadian route. Then, and not till then, will goods be shipped by an all-Canadian route. Such a route could be secured, an all-Canadian route, cheaper than any American route, for one-sixth the money it is proposed to spend upon this great Canadian transcontinental railway.
The hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) talked a great deal about the cheap railway haul from Chicago to New York. I would ask permission to submit to the House a statement from the record of the Chicago board of trade of the shipments of wheat and corn at that port for the season of 1901, of the average freight charges per bushel between Chicago and New York by lake and rail, and all-rail routes, and a statement of the summer traffic between Chicago and ocean ports. Thus, you see by these figures that a great deal of freight is shipped from Chicago to New York, some by water and rail and some all-rail, but in every case, the water transportation is very much cheaper. I would also like to read to the House the rate of freight from Buffalo to Liverpool in 1901. That rate was 111 cents from Buffalo, while from western Ontario it was 21 cents per 100 lbs. What I am trying to explain to the House and to the country is that by cheapening transportation a great deal of money may

be made for tlie farmers, the producers and the manufacturers of this country, if we were to improve these waterways so that we could get the same freight rate enjoyed by the people to the south of us. Last year it was stated that if the Americans had had to pay as high a rate of freight on goods shipped in the United States as we 'had to pay in Canada, they would have to pay on the amount of freight they shipped over $200,000,000 more than they did pay. That, Sir, would build the Grand Trunk Pacific in one year if we had as much freight to ship as they have. May I call attention to the comparative rate on cattle from American and Canadian points to the seaboard. Prom Toronto to Portland the rate on cattle is 28 cents; from Chicago to Portland, 800 miles greater distance, the rate is the same, 28 cents; from Chicago to Montreal the rate is 25 cents ; and from points in the county of Perth, Bruce or Huron to Montreal it is 33 cents, or 8 cents more than it is from Chicago to Montreal. You can see for yourself, Mr. Speaker, that is a very important, a very serious matter, not for the people who are going to come in and inhabit this new country seven or eight years hence, but to the people who are now here, and that is why I am so anxious to see a reduction in freight rates. To give a concrete case, Sir, the rate on cattle from the towrn of Listowel, in the constituency which I represent, is $1.25 per head higher to Montreal than from Chicago to Montreal, although from Chicago the haul is 400 miles longer than from Listowel.
In 1901 the United States shipped 500,000 head of cattle to England. If they had paid the same rate of freight that we pay in Canada, it would have cost them $500,000 more.
I might talk for hours along these lines, illustrating the need of reform in this direction, but I do not intend to take up much more of the time of this House. Thefe is one thing, however, that I wish to speak about. Hon. gentlemen talk about running freight by train through to the Atlantic coast from Portage la Prairie, Brandon, Indian Head, and all the great grain-producing centres of the North-west. But when a car leaves any of these points in the fall it does not return to the west for a month and that is one reason why I say it is necessary to have proper elevators built at the head of Lake Superior. You can run a car many times between Brandon and the head of Lake Superior while it is making one run through to the coast and return.
It would require an immense amount of rolling stock to handle that trade in that way. I hope the time is not far distanti when the government will build these elevators. There are immense elevators in Minneapolis and St. Paul. I saw one a few days ago in Minneapolis built entirely of cement, and this material could be utilized
by the government in building elevators at the head of Lake Superior. The farmers could ship their grain to these elevators, and receive in return warehouse receipts, upon which they could obtain money from the banks. If the government would do something of this kind, and drop this expensive scheme, involving an expenditure of $150,000,000, they would better serve the real interests of the country.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a long speech, which I think would be out of place at this stage of the debate. A great many members have been trespassing upon your kindness and upon the kindness of the House by taking advantage of this debate to introduce all sorts of subjects which are not relevant to the question before the House. I am going to follow the example of the hon. gentleman who has preceded me, and make my remarks very short. I think by this time the members of the House have made up their minds which way they are going to vote. There are sufficient facts and figures before the House to enable any man who takes the trouble to look into them(. to form a judgment, and a sound judgment on the question. Therefore, I have agreed with the whip on the other side of the House not to speak more than ten minutes, and if the hon. members who follow me will do the same, we shall get through this debate all the sooner, for your good, Mr. Speaker, for the good of the members and for the good of the country.
The principle of having a transcontinental railway line is admitted, so much so that the hon. leader of the opposition himself announces that the policy of the Conservative party is to have a transcontinental line. The discussion then, comes down to the method to be adopted for the building of that line. We have a proposition submitted by the government and a kind of proposition submitted by the opposition. As I do not want to give a silent vote, I desire to state in a few minutes why I favour the one scheme rather than the other.
This question of a transcontinental railway involves a question of transportation, a question of colonization, and, as the right Won. leader of the government has said, also a patriotic question-a question of transportation by attempting to relieve the congestion in the wTestern plains, to regulate the rates, and to give the farmers the benefit of low rates; a question of colonization, by opening new fields, and bringing in settlers to develop the natural resources of the northern country : and a patriotic question by having an all-Canadian line to carry Canadian products over Canadian territory to Canadian ports, and that. Sir, not only for six months in the year, as the scheme of the hon. leader of the opposition proposes, but for twelve months in the year.

la dealing with this question of transportation, some lion, members seemed to think that the only thing we have to transport from the western fields to the Atlantic seaboard is wheat. They do not take into consideration that there are ranchers on our western plains who raise cattle. They do not take into consideration the fact that though during the last few years we have had good crops in the North-west, there are other years when the crops are not so good. I remember, when I was. in the North-west in the late eighties and the early nineties, and when the crops failed, the general advice given to the farmers was to go into mixed farming. What does that involve V It involves the raising of cattle, and that the dairying industry will develop. It has been admitted by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), who professes to have made a special study of the transportation question, that cattle cannot be properly transported by being carried by train to Port Arthur, and there put on vessels and carried down the lakes and the St. Lawrence, but that they must be shipped by railway.
Now, what is the scheme proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition ? He proposes to buy from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company a portion of their line which is most unprofitable, a line which is mostly curves and grades, and which runs through a country where you can see, in place of vegetation, only burnt trees sticking out of rocks. He proposes to buy that line and pay millions of dollars for it. How is that going to relieve the congestion in the Northwest and help to bring the trade of the west to our Atlantic seaports ? The hon. gentleman proposes to make that line a common highway, over which the Grand Trunk Railway will obtain an entrance into the Northwest. He also proposes the purchase of the Canada Atlantic Railway, and by that means run the Intercolonial over this common highway. What would be the result V The result would be that all these lines would be able to carry traffic to Port Arthur and Fort William during the summer months, where the traffic would be transshipped to barges and sent down the lakes and the St. Lawrence to the Atlantic ocean. But what would be done in the winter ? The Grand Trunk Railway would take part of the traffic, and, instead of carrying it to Canadian ports,, when it reached Montreal, it will go on to Portland. Consequently the scheme of the hon. leader of the opposition involves this result, that for six months in the year the Grand Trunk Railway would carry Canadian produce through Canadian territory down to American ports. The proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition adds absolutely nothing to the transportation facilities of the country, but it involves handing so many millions of dollars over to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company Mr. BUREAU.
to put into their pockets, and so many millions to the Canada Atlantic Company.
The scheme evolved by the government, on the other hand, proposes to open up a new territory, to develop the natural resources of the country, to induce immigration to come in. The hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) the other day answered this argument by saying that he had from a reliable source the information that the territory now opened up in the west and covered by railways could accommodate 5,000,000 people. Well, Sir, it may accommodate 5,000,000 people, but it will not do so except on one condition. If a settler goes into a country that is already pretty well settled and where he has railway facilities, he must have a certain amount of capital to establish himself. He has to pay higher for the land, perhaps from $5 to $8 an acre ; he won't live in a sod house when he sees his neighbour occupying a substantial residence, and he must have better stock and better surroundings generally, than he would think of procuring were he settling in a new country. Now, when a pioneer settles in these newly opened up regions, the first year he can cut coird-wood, and' haul logs, ,and make a little money, and gradually he finds that he has his farm cleared and ready for cultivation. These are some advantages of settling in a new country, which favour the poorer settler, and they are not to be despised. I was also surprised to hear the leader of the Quebec Conservatives (Mr. Monk) speaking in the name of his province, say, that the line proposed by the government would run through subArctic regions and through a barren and desolate country. Let me tell him that north of the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec, in the counties of Portneuf, St. Maurice, Maskinonge, Berthier, Joliette and Montcalm through which this railway will run, the hon. member (Mr. Monk) makes a big mistake when he refers to them as subArctic regions or barren lands. There is no richer region in the Dominion of Canada than is this particular region I have spoken of. We have there vast water-powers, which are to-day neglected. Members of this House remember that when they visited Shawinigan Falls a couple of years ago. they saw for themselves some of the enormous water-powers of the St. Maurice river and the further you go north the more abundant these water-powers become. I am told by experts who have gone into that country for the Quebec government, that the La Tuque Falls which are 60 miles north east of Grand-M8re can develop unlimited power. Our friends opposite are talking about high tariff, and about the bringing in of manufactured products from the United States ; but let me tell them that manufacturing will go where it gets sufficient and cheap power to operate it. South of the

St. Lawrence river, where the leader of the opposition wants to run a railroad, you hardly have a water-power at all, but on the north, on the Gatineau river, the Li&vre river, the River St. Maurice, and the Matta-win, there is sufficient water-power to drive the wheels of industry of every manufacturing concern that can possibly settle in Canada. If you open up that country to the north, then instead of sending your trade to the United States as the scheme of the leader of the opposition would do, you will see settlers going in there, you will see manufacturing industries being developed there, and you will see that country the home of a numerous and a contented people. Five years ago the Shawinigan Falls and Grand-M&re were in a wilderness -to-day Grand-Mere has a population of 5,000 and Shawinigan Falls, after four years, a population of 3,000. I have no doubt that six years ago the member for Jacques Cartier would describe both Shawinigan and Grand-Mfere as being in a sub-Arctic and barren country. Let me say that there have been $5,000,000 invested in these two great water-powers on the St. Maurice river within the last four years. I felt somewhat ashamed to hear an hon. gentleman of the position and standing of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) belittle the northern part of the province of Quebec, in order to try and justify himself for opposing a scheme which he knows to be in the best interest of Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, my ten minutes are nearly up and as I will not break my word to you I have but a few sentences to add. By building this transcontinental line we will open up fertile regions through new Ontario. We have 16,000,000 acres there and we will develop them and bring them under cultivation. In Quebec a splendid territory will be developed by this railway which will be the home of manufacturing for Canada, just as New England is for the United States. We have in that country cheap water-powers sufficient to drive the wheels of industry and manufacture, and we will have availing of these water-powers thriving industries which will produce for the western farmers all the manufactured goods they are able to consume. I need not refer to the fertility of the Peace River district, for we are all agreed as to that. I am in favour of this scheme proposed by the government because it is a patriotic scheme. I am in favour of this scheme because it will carry Canadian trade through Canadian territory twelve months in the year, I am in favour of this scheme because it will develop the resources of our own country and attract settlers to us, I am in favour of the scheme because it is a grand national scheme promulgated by a wise government headed by a great statesman.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
speechtext:
I congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) upon the brevity with which he has stated all that can be said in support of this scheme, and I do so all the more heartily because he has done in ten minutes which it took the Finance Minister and the Minister of the Interior each five hours to accomplish. Hon. gentleman on both sides must realize that the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Bureau) has been a very useful contribution to the debate, when we remember the lengthy speeches we were forced to listen to from members on the Liberal side, who knew no more about the question than the hon. member for Three Rivers does. I must, however, say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bureau) has made the same argument as that used by all of the government supporters, including the ministers of the Crown who have spoken on this question. He told us that this scheme is a patriotic scheme, and that it is needed for transportation purposes, but he did not refer at all to the resolution now before the House ; which as most hon. gentlemen seem to have! forgotten, I shall read. This is it:
That it is expedient, in connection with the Bill now before this House, respecting the construction ot a national transcontinental railway, to ratify the agreement set forth in the schedule to the said Bill, entered into on the 28th of July, 1903, between the government and certain persons on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, a company to be incorporated by parliament at the present session thereof, and to authorize the government to do whatever is necessary to give full effect to the said Bill and agreement.
Now, Sir, I have not heard from the government or their supporters one word to prove that it is expedient to ratify this agreement. They seem to assume that because they allege it is a patriotic scheme and that we need transportation facilities, that therefore no matter what the price, the money shall be taken out of the pockets of the people to provide these facilities, and that it follows as a consequence that it is expedient to do so. I should consider that this expediency was similar to the expediency which the executor of an estate would adopt if he had in mind the conserving of that estate in the best interest of those to whom it belongs. I would consider expediency, that care which would dictate to the trustee that he should see that the bargain he is making is a good one, and that he is paying no more for what he gets than he ought to pay. I have listened attentively to this debate and I have heard little indeed as to why this scheme is expedient in the sense in which I understand the proper meaning of the term. It is my duty to draw the attention of gentlemen opposite to the fact that if this bargain is not a good bargain for the people of Canada, the patriotic side of it is not one which we should consider very seriously. We Conservatives do not need any lesson in patriotism from gentlemen on the other side. There was a time when we did not hear so much from

these gentlemen about a scheme being a Canadian scheme, or about a scheme freeing us from the bondage of the United States. There are gentlemen on the Liberal benches to-night who occupied seats here when blue ruin was the talk of the Liberal party, and when they contended that Canadian affairs would better be regulated from Washington. Things of that kind were said by the Liberals until the people of Canada became disgusted, and while we may congratulate these politicians that at last they have come to recognize that national questions must be dealt with from a Canadian standpoint, yet we must remember that the people sent us here to make the best bargain we can in their interests, and in the interest of the country. In every speech made on that side of the House we have had this menace of the abrogation of the bonding privilege repeated over and over] again. This, if it were not an insult to Canadian manhood, I would call a red-herring drawn across the trail in order to conceal from us the fact that the bargain is a mighty bad one.
On this resolution itself we did not hear from the right hon. the First Minister. He was probably within his rights when he nodded his head as you, Mr. Speaker, put the resolution to the House; and we have therefore to hark back to what he said on the Bill itself in order to find out the reasons he gave why this agreement should be ratified. Naturally, before deciding whether this was a wise and prudent bargain or not, the first thing we would ask of the right hon. gentleman is, where is your evidence of its acceptability ? What have you got to show that this is a good bargain for the people ? Well, after the right hon. gentleman had stated his case, we found a former colleague of his-one under whose particular administration this project would have naturally fallen, but who preferred to resign his seat in the cabinet rather than give it his endorsation-rising in his place and, in an argument which covered the whole ground, and which lasted some two hours and a half, putting the right hon. gentleman out of court. We found his former colleague proving that it was a most dangerous, improper, unsafe and absolutely foolish bargain. So convincingly did he state the case against the government, that the government have found it necessary to prolong this debate, in order to give every one of their supporters, on whom they could possibly count to make any kind of a plea in support of this scheme, an opportunity to reply to the strictures of the hon. the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. The ex-minister was the first witness to prove that this was a most expensive bargain. He told us, and his figures have not been controverted, that this projected road was going to cost us in the neighbourhood of $120,000,000 or $130,000,000. It is true that the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who was Mr. LANCASTER.
put up by the government to reply, undertook to show that an expenditure of $70,000,000 would cover the cost, but he did not go into the details, and he did not cover the whole of the project at all when he gave those figures. Contrast these estimates. We have first the estimate of the right hon. the First Minister, made upon the introduction of the Bill connected with this resolution, that the road was going to cost $13,000.000 and not a cent more. It is rather a striking commentary on the administrative ability of the First Minister, that the first witness against him was his former colleague, the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, a gentleman who was high in his counsels and respect until he disagreed with him upon this question. And we had the ex-minister-whose experience and knowledge in railway matters would entitle his opinion as an expert to much greater value than that of the right hon. gentleman-declaring that the cost, instead of being $13,000.000. would be $120,000,000 or $130,000,000. This was rather hard testimony for the right hon. gentleman to refute; and it is evident how hard pressed he was when he had to solicit the aid, in order to bolster up the case of the government, of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who, as this House well knows, is prepared to argue convincingly on either side of any question, just as his interests of the moment dictate. Well, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) estimated the cost at $68,000,000 or $70,000,000-considerably less than that of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, but considerably greater than that of the First Minister. Then we had the hon. the Finance Minister brought to the rescue, and that hon. gentleman went the Premier one better, and reduced the cost from $13,000,000 to $8,000,000. Could we require any better proof than these contradictory estimates, furnished by the principal supporters of this bargain, by the promoters of it, to show that the government are really rushing into this vast undertaking without having the faintest idea of what it is really going to cost the people. Following the Finance Minister, we have had any number of gentlemen on the government side giving us estimates varying from $120,000,000 down to $8,000,000. Of the lot, the hon. the Finance Minister is the most penurious, the most anxious to make the figures as small as possible, and we are expected to find our way out of all this maze and come to a decision on which we can rely with any degree of certainty. All we have to go by is what evidence and information we can glean from the present debate; and if this discussion were to last three months instead of three weeks-aye if it were to last three years instead of three weeks-the people would be better satisfied than to let the contract go through with no other than the meagre information submitted to us. The opposition. Sir, would be false to their

duty if they did not keep up this debate, if for no other reason than to obtain every possible scrap of information we can possibly secure before committing the country to this extravagant project. In the course of three weeks which this debate has lasted, we have been given no reliable information as to what this project is going to cost. We are still completely in the dark as to the amount of liability we are about to impose on the country. For that reason alone my constituents-those who voted against me as well as those who voted for me-would consider that I had done wrong if 1 did not make every effort to obtain for the country more information before allowing this resolution to go through. Even those who voted against me at my election would be justified in saying :	' Although we did vote
against you, we expected, when you did go to Ottawa, that you would find out what you are called upon to vote for, before giving your vote, and if you cannot do that we will get somebody who will. And they would be quite right. For my part I cannot understand how any lion, gentleman can take the position taken by the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Hr. Bureau), of declaring that as this resolution was proposed by the government he was supporting, he was going to vote for it without any regard for its merits or the consequences. That is not the position we on this side take. We want to find out all about a question before casting our votes either for or against any proposition submitted to us.
The right hon. the First Minister gave us four reasons why this scheme should go through. First, he said, he wanted it to carry grain. It seems to me, however, that my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) rather gave the real reason when he said that it was not to carry grain the Premier wanted the road but to carry the elections. But for my part, I am confident that the elections will not be carried, as the hon. the First Minister intends they shall, and the people will once more put the Conservative party back into office, because that is the party which is willing to do what is right. I do not believe that the few millionaires, which the right hon. gentleman hopes to construct out of this scheme at the expense of the people, will be powerful enough to carry the elections. I have too much faith in the integrity and independence of the people to believe that all the millions which can be raised out of this scheme by the half a dozen millionaires it is going to create will be able to carry the election. It is an insult to the intelligence of the people to suppose that they will not see through a scheme of this kind and that they will be carried away by such corrupt and clumsy devices in this year of grace, 1903.
The second reason which the First Minister gave for asking this House to pass this resolution was that the scheme would
only cost the people $13,000,000. I have shown how he has been put out of court by his own witness on that point and will not trouble the House by further discussing it. And he gave a third reason, that with regard to the bonding privilege. I feel like apologizing for even mentioning that matter in this House. It was a trashy argument to be put forward by anybody, and it has been exploded by every speaker on this side who has dealt with it, and has been dropped by hon. gentlemen opposite like a hot iron or-well, I hardly know what comparison to offer, because it has been a quicker and more impulsive letting go than anything I can think of in ordinary life. I notice hon. gentlemen opposite have not referred to the bonding privilege question since the address of the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell). That hon. gentleman has courage far greater than his stature. I must say this for the hon. gentleman-he can speak for four or five hours, and in ten minutes he can use more words than most of the rest of us can use in twice the time. But that hon. gentleman did so thoroughly explode the arguments of those on his own side with regard to the bonding privilege that I feel sure that none of the others will deal with it. I do not think, for instance, that the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), who is the only member of the government present and the only one who seems to think it necessary to pay any more attention to this debate-on which I congratulate him-will try to revamp this bonding privilege argument. If he is to speak in this debate, I should be glad indeed if he, as a man of business experience, and one who must know a great deal about the shipping and handling of freights on railways, steamboats and in every other way that goods are transhipped, would corroborate, if he can, some of the arguments of the hon. member for Hants when speaking on this question. I think the country also would be very glad to receive his views upon it. No doubt, the hon. gentleman will say that the bonding privilege has nothing to do with the question. The right hon. Prime Minister quoted a statement made by the President of the United States-he did not say when, but I think it was fourteen or fifteen years ago-a statement evidently made for election purposes. It was just like any one of the many efforts in the United States to twist the British lion's tail made just before the election, in order to please a certain element and win its votes. In the same way, President Cleveland, seeking to be re-elected, made his threat as to what he was going to do to us poor Canucks with regard to the bonding privilege, I thought the fact of the Prime Minister referring to this utterance was very suggestive. For, just after talking this kind of nonsense, Mr. Cleveland went to the country and was overwhelmingly defeated. I think that when the Prime Minister appeals to the people and they see that this bonding

privilege talk is all that lie knows about the expediency of the contract lie asks them to confirm, tfiey will tell liim lie had better accept the same verdict that Mr. Cleveland got, as he seems to know just as -much about the bonding privilege and the transportation business as Mr. Cleveland did. As to the speech of the hon. member for Hants, I think that those who heard it-though I could hardly blame any hon. gentleman who did not hear it at all, because it took up half of one day and pretty nearly the whole of the next until evening-will agree with me that if that speech is printed and circulated it will convince the people that they ought to vote for the party who oppose this legislation, and not for the party on whose behalf the hon. gentleman (Mr. Russell) was speaking. He gave some very strange arguments in support of the resolution. He acknowledged the fact-as will be found on referring to page 9235 of the current ' Hansard '-that the building of this line from Quebec to Moncton would probably have the effect of turning the Intercolonial Railway over to the scrap iron heap. Referring to that point, he said that a new invention or appliance took the place of the old, and the change is beneficial to the community at large. He instanced certain manufactures, and said that one manufacture took the place of another, and so, as one railway became inefficient another would have to be constructed ; and if the construction of the new road-and there he was referring to the Quebec and Moncton line-had the effect of reducing the Intercolonial to the scrap iron heap, it did not make any difference, because we should have a better road. There was a distinct admission that the seventy millions of dollars spent on the Intercolonial are of no account.
I know-and I have been aware ,of it, perhaps, longer than some hon. gentlemen on the other side-that, taking them as a whole, the people of Canada are not a stingy people. The people of Canada are ready to pay and pay pretty well, for anything they require in the interest of the country. But when an hon. gentleman representing a constituency in this House tosses aside seventy million dollars of their money as of no account, says that it may be thrown in the scrap heap, and calls the institution on which the money has been spent a mere ' raft in the shipwreck '- those were his words when he said that the Intercolonial as compared with the whole transportation question was a mere 'raft in the shipwreck '-I think the people of Canada will say to him that it seems to be a pretty dear raft, that it is made of the most expensive kind of timber, and that the pieces, instead of being fastened together with iron bars, are fastened together with gold plate. On this road we are asked this session to vote $3,000,000, for what ? The other day the Governor General consented Mr. LANCASTER.
to a Supply Bill covering one-fifth of the
estimates for the current year, these having been passed by arrangement between the leaders in this House. The remaining four-fifths of these various items still remain for discussion. And this total of $3,000,000 to be spent on the Intercolonial is for what ? It is for betterments. The government propose to spend this amouut of money to put the road in more perfect condition than it is in to-day. The right hon. Premier gave the key note for the chorus of his followers with regard to the Intercolonial when, in introducing this Bill, he said that the Intercolonial was built for military purposes and not for purposes of transportation. The hon. member for Hants took courage from that, and went on to call the Intercolonial a 'raft in a shipwreck.' Yet this is the road upon which this government in its seven years of office has spent $20,000,000. And now, we are told the weeds should be allowed to grow up on the Intercolonial, and the rails, perhaps, be sold as scrap iron, and the whole institution allowed to go to waste. Yet, while this is looked to as the result of that policy they propose to spend $3,000,000 to still further improve the Intercolonial.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) when he considered the improvidence and outrageousness of the scheme used very mild language when he talked about hysterical frenzy or temporary madness as having surely had something to do in dictating this policy. How could any hon. gentleman who had the least respect for himself, who valued the good opinion of those whom he met day by day, and joined with the Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen supporting the government in voting these millions every year, including the part of this $3,000,000 already voted this session, thus declaring that the Intercolonial should be kept with the top notches railways-how could he at the same time support a scheme which involved the idea that the Intercolonial was not fit for the purposes of a railway and was so regarded by the government.
What are the facts. Mr. Speaker? Does any one doubt that the Intercolonial is fit for the purpose? Is it not doing all the business that it can do or that can be done by any railway? Is it not reasonable that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) should urge that the Intercolonial should be used as far as it goes and that it should be extended, as he suggests, up to the great lakes in order to afford the transportation facilities that are there required. Is it not reasonable that we should avoid the absolute waste of paralleling the road which we already own, paralleling it and paralysing it by building a commercial enemy. That is the proposition of the government, and it is one that should be condemned, while I submit that the alternative proposi-

tion of the leader of the opposition, so far as the Intercolonial is concerned, is one that must commend itself to this country.
The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell), one of the principal supporters of the government, also distinctly said that it did not matter to him whether the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), in leaving the government, was actuated by high conviction or by resentment. Let us look at the state of political morality which this indicates. It mattered not to him whether it was from honest conviction that a matter was wrong and ought not to be forced upon the country, that the hon. ex-minister abandoned his office, gave up its emoluments, and left the cabinet councils of the country, or whether he did it in a pet, angry at some imaginary rebuff he had received. What conditions are we coming to in this House ? Are we going to vote things simply because the right hon. the Prime Minister says we are to do so? Because he bows to you, Mr. Speaker, as much as to say: Enough said; that is my resolution; I desire it to pass; what right has the country to know what my evidence is in support of it ? I am Premier, I bow to you as a token that I want that to pass; that settles it-it must be passed, and the people of this country and the opposition are not entitled to know any more than I choose to tell them as to whether it is expedient or not.
As representing a somewhat prominent constituency, one with over 30,000 people, I protest. I want some evidence in justification of the expenditure of this money before I can bring my conscience to consent or before I believe the consciences of the people I represent would consent to this deal-for it is nothing but a deal-going through.
The fourth reason, and the Premier touched a good many times on it-and with all respect, I wish to say I was astonished at his hardihood-that this railway must be built was because the Conservative party once made a pledge that they would do something of the same kind, and that he thought he should redeem the pledge of the Conservative party. Charity begins at home, and if there is any charity in a Reform government, it should begin there too. We do not ask the Premier to pay our debts; we have had no claims filed against the Conservative party and proved in the ordinary way, to show that there are any debts of this kind against the Conservative party. We know, however, that there are a good many claims to be satisfied by the Reform party, who in 1890 turned out of office better men than they are, by making pledges they did not intend to carry out. To show how callous this government are in the matter of broken pledges, I would remind the House that in the speech from the Throne, placed in the mouth of His Excellency by this government, a pledge was made that this question would be dealt
with in a very different way, and we have heard no apology as to why that pledge was not carried out. I would advise the right hon. gentleman to pay his debts, so recent and so fresh in the minds of the people, before he talks such nonsense as he has talked about the debts of the Conservative party. I tell him, without fear of contradiction, that the Conservative party does not owe a single debt on account of broken pledges and does not want any advice from any Premier of any so-called Reform government.
To do the hon. Prime Minister credit he said that it was for patriotic reasons that it was essentia] that this railway should be built. If I understand my constituency and the province of Ontario, and in fact all the constituencies of the Dominion of Canada-for I do not understand that one Canadian is different from another in his knowledge of patriotism and of his business duty-I believe thoroughly that the people of Canada want the business which we are sent here with a solemn trust to conduct, dealt with on its merits and without any such nonsense as patriotism being used as a reason for a bad Bill going through. What patriotism is there in making five or six millionaires at the expense of the people? Have we to constitute Morgans and Vanderbilts and Rockfellers, five or six of them, before we can call ourselves a nation, before we can wake up and find ourselves a nation? Has the Premier to go to sleep again and have another dream and find that we are not a nation because we have no multi-millionaires ? We are sent here as the representatives of the people to look after their interests, and it is not fair to-take from every family of five what this scheme will take. It will cost in round numbers 8150,000,000, with no interest and no return, and it is not fair to thus assess every poor man's family $150 in order to make five or six millionaires.
No case has been made out in support of this scheme. The Conservative party does not stop short at criticism. They would be justified in saying : Because you have not proved to this House that this measure is expedient, therefore we must assume it is not expedient. The Conservative party have investigated the facts; they have said to themselves and to the people, If the government will not ascertain the facts and take the trouble to have surveys and plans made and to ,see what they are doing, we will do it. although we have not such facilities as the government have, although the expenses we make will come ;out of our pockets and not out of the public exchequer, although every telegram we send and every engineer and every explorer we employ, must be paid out of our own pockets-although all this is so, still, in the interest of the country, we will ascertain what this is going to be. And so at considerable expense, and at the cost of a great deal of

time and energy, we have shown to you and to the House and to this government- if they will be good enough to open their ears wide enough to take it in-what this is going to amount to.
What does it amount to? It is going to cost $150,000,000, and the canals of the country are going to be rendered useless if the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite is good. I do not think their arguments are good in that respect. I think the canals will still do business, 'but I do not think this railway will do the business that hon. gentlemen opposite pretend it will do. If their arguments are good this road ought to be able to handle all the traffic and the canals are to be put out of business. The scores of millions of dollars which have been spent in the building of our canals are to be wasted the moneys spent on the Georgian bay are to be wasted, the moneys spent on the St. Lawrence canal system are to be wasted, if their arguments are good, because according to these hon. gentlemen this railway is going to do more than any other railway can do. It is pretended by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that this railway will be able to carry thei grain from the west and that another railway cannot do it. It is a strange thing that this railway should possess a supernatural power to do that which these hon. gentlemen say other railways cannot do. If these hon. gentlemen are correct in what they say, then the canals and the existing railways are all bad, and if they are not, this particular railway will be no good. The Canadian Pacific Railway is not able to carry, according to their argument, any such quantities of grain from the west as this railway is going to carry under similar conditions, though the trains are hauled by the same kind of engines and through the same kind of country. The argument of these hon. gentlemen is that unless this particular railway is constructed the grain cannot be carried out of the country, because hon. gentlemen say that this railway can do what other railways cannot do. The proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition has all the advantages that the government scheme assumes to possess and at one-third of the expense. There is no question but that all the grain can be brought out and that the fruit from the eastern provinces can be sent up to the west. I was amused to hear the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) talk about shipping his apples and other fruits to Great Britain. Does he not know that we cannot send our apples and other fruit from the Niagara district to Winnipeg because the freights are too high to allow us to do it ? The miller in the North-west Territories gets his barrel of flour carried to St. Catharines for less than one-half the freight that the fruitgrower has to pay to get his barrel of apples carried up to Winnipeg. Do the people in the hon. gentleman's county want to send Mr. LANCASTER.
their fruit to Great Britain or to the west ? If they want to be national In their ideas let them start to build up a trade at home. Does the hon. gentleman not think that hon. gentlemen who sit in this House, that the friends and relations of hon. gentlemen who sit in this House, and that the people of Canada should be considered a little in this question as well as himself and those he speaks for ? I am not going to say that because the farmers of Ontario had to build granaries in the pioneer days, that because they had to take care of their grain until the railways were built, that because they had to hold it for months and months ; that because in the early days of Ontario the farmers did not have the advantages that are now afforded to the people of the west, we should not give these advantages to the western people. The section of the country which I have the honour to represent is not stingy and it does not object to any proper bargain that is entered into in regard to railways, but if the country is going to build railways, build them on a sensible plan ; do not build them and then hand them over to a corporation at the expense of the people who get no benefit from them.
I want to say one word in regard to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce IRt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). The right hon. gentleman made a speech upon this question the other day. Of course, if the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) does not agree with the scheme, the next best man to appeal to is the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), because it is a money question. The hon. gentleman said that the whole cost would be for the interest, which amounts to $8,000,000, but he did not tell us what it would cost for the payment of the prinicpal. The next hon. gentleman that we would be apt to call upon to give us some information in regard to this project is the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. The right hon. gentleman addressed a long speech on this question to this House, or rather to the other side of the House. During the course of this debate I have noticed that when cabinet ministers undertake to address the House on the subject they turn their backs upon you, Mr. Speaker, and upon the people of the country as represented by the opposition, and they devote their attention to trying to convince their own followers that they had better vote for this scheme. It is quite evident that the cabinet ministers from the right hon. Premier down are afraid to trust the fidelity of hon. gentlemen sitting behind them, and therefore, whilst endeavouring to convince their own supporters, they turn their backs upon you,, Mr. Speaker, and upon us. because they think it does not make any difference about us if they can only hold the fifty' majority which they have had since 1900. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to convince the hon.

gentlemen behind him. He told us nothing whatever about the present project, but he said that if the late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie's scheme had gone on the country would have been more prosperous in 1885 than it is now. I do not know. I may be stupid, but if that is the case I do not know why it is that we have not 15,000,000 or 20,000,000 people here now, although I am sure this country has enjoyed a large measure of prosperity since 1878, when Mr. Mackenzie was put out of power because he was considered by the people not to be able to carry on the affairs of the country in such a way as to promote its prosperity. I am sure it has prospered since and if the same proportion was to be given effect to we would get ourselves into that same maze that the hon. gentlemen on the other side have got themselves into when trying to show us that this is a good scheme. He did tell us he was afraid that in the face of our record we would not be able to make it go down with the people that this was not a good thing for the country. I recall the time three years ago next November when the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce came over to St. Catharines to defeat me and to endeavour to have the present Senator Gibson elected by a good majority. He made a speech in the Opera House in St. Catharines and he undertook to speak in regard to the fiscal policy. His speech on that question was about as applicable to the fiscal policy as his speech In this House the other day was applicable to this railway project. He made about the same kind of 9 speech in comparison as he made here the other day, and the result was that a majority in 1896 of 119 was converted into a majority in 1900 of 396. I can assure the hon. minister that if he comes over at the next election he will save me a lot of trouble and a lot of election expenses. If he will come over to the Opera House in St. Catharines and deliver the same kind of a speech upon the railway policy that he delivered In regard to the fiscal policy on the occasion to which il have referred, I think he will increase my majority from 369 to probably 1,069.
I was going to speak for a moment in regard to the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), who addressed the House upon this question yesterday. He said that he had listened very carefully to the speeches delivered during this debate, that he had read ' Hansard ' containing what he had not listened to, and that he had not heard one word uttered by any hon. gentleman on this side of the House taking any exception to the paralleling of the Intercolonial Railway. Here is an hon. gentleman speaking in this House trying to belittle the arguments of the opposition and stating that no hon. gentleman on this side of the House has found fault with this road because it is paralleling the Intercolonial Railway. Tlie hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell), 311
who spoke a little while before him, had taken up an hour or more with his argument in respect to the bonding privilege and he had devoted another hour and a half in trying to convince the House that the paralleling of the Intercolonial Railway was not in reality a paralleling of the Intercolonial Railway, but a paralleling of the Grand Trunk Pacific by the Intercolonial Railway. That is about the way he left the matter when he got through with it, and ,then he said that the effect of it was that if the Intercolonial Railway were turned into scrap iron it would not make any difference.
I would advise the hon. member for (Welland) Mr. German to consult the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) as an eye and ear specialist, so that when he reads ' Hansard ' again and listens to the debates in this House, he will understand better what has been said. The hon. gentleman (Mr. German) could not give any reason to the people of Ontario as to why $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 should be wasted in paralleling the Intercolonial Railway, towards the construction of which the ratepayers of that province have contributed largely. He knew that if the new line paralleled the Intercolonial Railway it should not be built, and then he resorted to the device of saying that he heard no one on this side of the House making objection to the paralleling. Well, if he listened he would have heard it. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) comes from the Niagara district-although not as good a part of it as I come from-it might be thought that if I did not refute what he said I had acquiesced in it. I am bound in the interests of the honest reformers and the Conservatives of that district to refute his statements at the first opportunity. He told us that he understood in the Railway Committee that no substantial assistance was to be given to the Grand Trunk Railway. I was in the committee when the Grand Trunk Railway Bill was being discussed, and I know that we had all we could do to keep gentlemen opposite from pledging the government that there would be no financial aid given to the company, if a charter were passed. They were afraid that the government would give financial assistance, and on the very preamble of the Bill, and all through its clauses they endeavoured to provide that there would be no financial assistance given to that company. We have heard from the Minister of the Interior, and we have heard from other gentlemen from the west, that the great cry in the North-west is that they cannot get trains enough to take the products of that country to the seaboard. If that be true, and I suppose it is, it would seem that a railway should give a bonus to the country for granting permission to enter that region. When a railway builds there, it is not a case of taking chances. Subsidies are paid to railways when they un-



dertake a venture which looks doubtful, but *which if successful may add to the prosperity of the country. Subsidies are paid to railways to open up countries so that crops may be grown and hauled out. But here is a country in which the trouble is that the existing railways cannot handle all the freight that is offered to them. Is that not a good reason why this railway in the prairie section, should not be subsidized, but on the contrary that it should be thankful to get permission to enter that country and to do the business which is waiting for it. The hon. gentleman from Welland (Mr. German) also told us that there was nothing in the contention that this new road would parallel the Intercolonial Railway, because if the government did not parallel the Intercolonial the Grand Trunk Railway would step in and do it itself. Well, I would point out to him that the Grand Trunk Railway could not build one foot of road to parallel the Intercolonial Railway unless parliament gave them a charter to do so. What idleness it is for the member for Welland to say that unless the government built this section of the road, the Grand Trunk Railway Company would build it and themselves parallel the Intercolonial Railway. Why, the Grand Trunk Railway cannot do any such thing unless they get a charter. They cannot build a foot of road unless they get a Dominion charter where it is to the general advantage of Canada or a provincial charter with respect to a portion of the road which affects only a particular province. The member for Welland says that we are lat the mercy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in this matter, when as a matter of fact the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway must and should be nt the mercy of parliament for any favours which they may get, or for any permission to build roads which they may obtain. Sir, the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals was absolutely correct when he talked about the hysterical frenzy of the government. You would imagine that they believed that the Grand Trunk Railway could take the people of Canada by the throat and say : Unless you build this railway from Quebec to Moncton, we will build it, and we will put your Intercolonial Railway out of business. That is the sort of argument that comes from the hon. member for Welland. Then the hon. gentleman told us that we had the advantage of government ownership in the road from Moncton to Winnipeg, because we will build the road ourselves. What is ownership in a railroad or in a House, or in a barn, or in anything else if it is not the right to use it; and has not the government of this country handed over the right to use that road and the practical ownership for fifty years ? What good is the title if we have not the user ? If the scheme of the leader of the opposition were adopted we would have the right to use the roads acquired, and therefore we

would have all the attributes of ownership; but in this case you build the road and for half a century you hand over what is practically its ownership to the Grand Trunk Pacific. It is not my habit to say what any man's constituency will stand from him. but if I know the people of Welland, I doubt very much if they will not resent the action of the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) in underestimating their intelligence to such an extent as to suppose that the arguments he has advanced to this House would appeal to any reasonable man.
The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German does not care what will happen fifty years hence and the member for Hants (Mr. Russell) told us that he was tired of hearing people talk of fifty years hence when he would be in his grave. Well, I should have thought that the Prime Minister would have given a little attention to this matter before he entered into this scheme. You cannot convince any business man in this country, nay, you cannot convince any schoolboy, that in a matter of national concern you must not look forward for fifty years. Why, Sir, this road will have made millionaires of its promoters or it will be found to be an utter failure in the jnext fifteen or twenty years. We know that railways which were constructed fifty years *ago are not doing business in the same way to-day as when they were first operated. How does any gentleman know in this age of scientific research and invention what the conditions will be fifty years hence ? I notice that charters which this government have passed speak about steam and electricity as being possibly set aside and their place taken by an atmospheric pressure or other discoveries as motor power. It may be that in handing this railway over to the Grand Trunk Pacific for fifty years we are handing it over for the time that it will be of any profit whatever.
